description: From plague prayers and flagellants to Jenner's vaccine — how Britain tried to prevent disease.
content_html:
Preventing Disease Before Science

Prevention is better than cure — but for most of history, people could not prevent what they could not understand. Medieval and early modern attempts to stop disease relied on the same incorrect theories that shaped their understanding of its causes: miasma, divine punishment and the four humours. Only from the eighteenth century onwards did more systematic, evidence-based approaches to prevention begin to appear.

Medieval Responses to the Black Death

When the Black Death struck England in 1348, communities tried a range of preventive measures. Flagellants travelled from town to town flogging themselves, convinced that demonstrating extreme suffering would show God they had repented. Towns introduced quarantine measures, sealing infected houses and sometimes entire streets. Bonfires were lit to burn away miasma; people carried posies of sweet-smelling herbs. Alchemists sold remedies claiming to drive out poison from the body. Soothsayers and astrologers advised on auspicious dates to avoid travel. None of these worked against a flea-borne bacterial infection, but they reflected the best understanding available at the time.

Key Fact

Medieval plague prevention included flagellation, quarantine, burning bonfires to purify air, carrying herbs, and seeking advice from alchemists and soothsayers. All these methods were based on miasma theory or belief in divine punishment — not on knowledge of bacteria or fleas.

Inoculation: A Significant Step, c.1700

The first genuinely effective approach to preventing a specific disease came not from a European physician but from the Ottoman Empire. Inoculation against smallpox was practised in the Middle East and China before it reached Britain. In 1721, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador to Constantinople, introduced the practice to British society after having her own children inoculated in Turkey. She had herself survived smallpox but lost her brother to it.

Inoculation involved transferring matter from a mild smallpox pustule into a healthy person. The person usually suffered a mild form of the disease, recovered, and was thereafter protected. It was risky — a small number of those inoculated died from the procedure — but far less dangerous than catching smallpox naturally. By the mid-eighteenth century, inoculation was used across parts of Britain, particularly among the wealthy.

The most important development in disease prevention before the twentieth century was made by Edward Jenner in 1796. Jenner, a doctor working in Gloucestershire, noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox — a mild disease affecting cattle and humans — rarely contracted smallpox. He hypothesised that the cowpox infection conferred protection against the deadlier disease. In May 1796 Jenner took matter from a cowpox pustule on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes and inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps. The boy developed a mild fever but recovered. Jenner then exposed Phipps to smallpox matter on multiple occasions; the boy showed no ill effects. Jenner published his findings in 1798 in a work titled An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae.

The procedure Jenner developed was named vaccination, from the Latin vacca meaning cow. It was safer than inoculation because it used a different, milder disease rather than smallpox itself. Jenner did not fully understand why it worked — germ theory and the concept of antibodies lay decades ahead — but he had shown through careful observation and testing that it did.

Spreading Vaccination: Resistance and Compulsion

Vaccination spread unevenly. Many doctors were sceptical; the medical establishment initially resisted Jenner’s claims. Religious opposition also emerged — some people objected to using animal material. Satirical cartoonists depicted vaccinated people growing horns and bovine features. Acceptance grew as evidence mounted. In 1840, inoculation was made illegal in Britain and vaccination against smallpox was offered free. In 1853, smallpox vaccination was made compulsory for all infants. In 1867, this was extended and fines introduced for non-compliance. Despite anti-vaccination protests, compulsory vaccination substantially reduced smallpox deaths in Britain.

Key Fact

Jenner used cowpox matter to vaccinate James Phipps in 1796, demonstrating protection against smallpox. Vaccination became compulsory for infants in 1853. Smallpox was eventually eradicated globally in 1980, the only human disease ever to be eliminated entirely.

The scientific explanation for why vaccination worked only came after germ theory had been established. In 1890, German scientists Emil von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato demonstrated that the blood of animals exposed to weakened diphtheria toxin contained substances that neutralised the toxin — the first identification of what we now call antibodies. This discovery won von Behring the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901. Understanding antibodies allowed scientists to develop increasingly targeted vaccines and, later, therapeutic anti-sera. It transformed the scientific basis of disease prevention from empirical observation to mechanistic understanding.

Change and Continuity in Disease Prevention

Looking across the period from 1500 to the present, the most significant change in disease prevention is the move from prayer and purification to scientifically validated immunisation programmes. Yet elements of continuity persist: quarantine — used against plague in 1348 — was still used during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Hesitancy about vaccination, recorded since Jenner’s time, remains a challenge for public health today. The factors that drove change included scientific progress (germ theory, bacteriology), government action (compulsory vaccination acts, public health legislation) and improvements in education and communication.
exam_tip_html: When answering a question about the significance of Edward Jenner, make sure you cover two levels: significance at the time (replaced dangerous inoculation; provided a safe way to prevent smallpox; led to compulsory vaccination by 1853) and significance over time (laid the foundation for all future vaccine development; contributed to the eventual global eradication of smallpox in 1980). Top-band answers address both, not just one. Avoid describing what Jenner did without explaining why it mattered.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval plague prevention — flagellation, quarantine, burning herbs — was based on miasma theory and divine punishment, not scientific understanding of infection.
  • Lady Mary Wortley Montagu introduced inoculation to Britain in 1721; Edward Jenner developed the safer practice of vaccination in 1796 using cowpox to protect against smallpox.
  • The discovery of antibodies by Behring and Kitasato in 1890 gave a scientific explanation for how immunity works, transforming disease prevention from observation-based practice to mechanistic science.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of medieval attempts to prevent the spread of plague.
practice_questions.marks: One feature supported with accurate detail. Example: Towns quarantined infected houses, sealing them shut to stop plague victims moving around and spreading disease to others. [2 marks: 1 for identifying a feature, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Edward Jenner's work on vaccination.
practice_questions.marks: Feature 1: Jenner vaccinated James Phipps in 1796 using cowpox matter, demonstrating that exposure to cowpox could protect against the more dangerous smallpox. Feature 2: Jenner published his findings in 1798, and his work eventually led to compulsory smallpox vaccination for infants in Britain by 1853. [2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why it took time for Jenner's vaccination to become widely accepted in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation with multiple linked reasons (medical scepticism, religious objections, satirical/cultural opposition) demonstrating why acceptance was slow. Secure: A clear reason with relevant explanation and evidence. Developing: A reason identified but explanation limited. Emerging: Simple statement that people were against it, no explanation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of inoculation and vaccination in the prevention of disease in Britain between 1700 and 1900.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (reducing smallpox deaths, replacing dangerous inoculation, enabling compulsory vaccination 1853) AND over time (foundation of all modern immunisation programmes, eradication of smallpox 1980). Secure: Significance at the time with evidence; some longer-term reference. Developing: One aspect of significance with limited evidence. Emerging: Basic description without significance analysis. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The work of Edward Jenner was the most important turning point in the prevention of disease in Britain.'
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees with evidence (safer than inoculation, led to compulsory vaccination, smallpox eradication) AND disagrees by weighing other turning points (germ theory enabling vaccines for other diseases; antibody discovery; public health legislation). Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides addressed with evidence, clear conclusion. Developing: One-sided argument with some evidence. Emerging: Descriptive with no evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text: How did the approach to preventing disease change between c.1350 and c.1900? Use evidence from across the period to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Traces change across all three eras (medieval: miasma/prayer/flagellants; early modern: inoculation introduced c.1721; modern: Jenner's vaccination 1796, compulsory vaccination 1853, antibody discovery 1890), weighs change against continuity (quarantine throughout all periods), reaches substantiated judgement. Secure: All three eras covered with evidence. Developing: Two eras, limited weighing. Emerging: Single era, descriptive only. [16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Who introduced the practice of inoculation against smallpox to British society in 1721?
What key difference made vaccination safer than inoculation?
options: Vaccination used a stronger dose of smallpox
Vaccination used a related but milder disease (cowpox) rather than smallpox itself
Vaccination was performed by trained surgeons only

knowledge_checks.q: Edward Jenner vaccinated James Phipps in _____, using matter from a cowpox pustule.
The discovery of _____ by Behring and Kitasato in 1890 provided a scientific explanation for how immunity works.
Match each person to their contribution to disease prevention:
right: Discovered antibodies in blood serum in 1890
Developed cowpox-based vaccination against smallpox in 1796

flashcard_questions.q: Who introduced inoculation against smallpox to Britain, and when?

flashcard_questions.a: Introducing a small amount of infectious material to produce a mild infection and confer future immunity.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Edward Jenner use to vaccinate James Phipps in 1796?
flashcard_questions.a: Matter from a cowpox pustule on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was vaccination safer than inoculation?
flashcard_questions.a: It used cowpox, a milder related disease, rather than smallpox itself.

flashcard_questions.q: When was smallpox vaccination made compulsory for infants in Britain?
Smallpox was the only human disease ever fully eradicated. When did this happen?
Who were the flagellants and why did they whip themselves during the Black Death?
flashcard_questions.a: Members of a religious movement who believed self-punishment would appease God and end the plague.

flashcard_questions.q: What did alchemists claim to offer as plague prevention?
flashcard_questions.a: Remedies claiming to drive out poison from the body using natural and supernatural forces.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the name Jenner gave to his new procedure, and what Latin word does it come from?
flashcard_questions.a: Vaccination, from 'vacca' — the Latin word for cow.

flashcard_questions.q: Who discovered antibodies in 1890, and what were they working on?
flashcard_questions.a: Emil von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato, studying diphtheria toxin.
Proteins produced by the immune system that neutralise specific pathogens and provide future immunity.

flashcard_questions.q: In which year did Jenner publish his findings on vaccination?

glossary_terms.definition: Members of a religious movement who whipped themselves publicly as an act of penance, believing this would appease God and end the plague.
Medieval practitioners who claimed to transform base metals into gold and cure disease through the manipulation of natural and supernatural forces.
A process of deliberately introducing a small amount of infectious material into a healthy person to produce a mild infection and confer future immunity.
The use of a weakened or related form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system to provide protection against disease, developed from the word 'vacca' (Latin for cow).
Proteins produced by the immune system in response to a specific pathogen, which neutralise it and provide future immunity.
